Maladaptive Strategies.value: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
There is something wrong with me as a person
I acted in ways that go against who I am

vignette: Rajiv's eyes scan the crowded coffee shop, his mind on high alert for any sign of danger. It's been two years since he was tortured by government forces while investigating a corruption scandal in his home country. The experience left him with a deep-seated fear that others can see the trauma etched on his face, like an invisible scar. He feels defective, as if there's something fundamentally wrong with him. As a journalist, Rajiv used to thrive in chaotic environments, but now the sounds of children crying or the faint hum of a generator can send him spiraling into a panic. When he hears these triggers, he's transported back to the dingy cell where he was held captive. He tries to recall the details of his ordeal, but his memories are hazy and fragmented. There are moments that feel unreal, like they happened to someone else. Other parts are shrouded in darkness, lost forever. Rajiv's response to these triggers is to withdraw from social interactions, avoiding friends and colleagues who might ask questions or try to offer support. He's convinced that they'll see the shame and guilt written all over his face, and he can't bear the thought of being pitied or judged. To cope with the anxiety that comes flooding in, Rajiv restricts his food intake, a maladaptive strategy that leaves him feeling weak and lightheaded. When he's out in public, Rajiv finds himself constantly scanning his surroundings, watching for potential threats. He's hyper-vigilant, always on edge, ready to pounce at the slightest sound. The dizziness only adds to his sense of disorientation, making it harder for him to focus. His mind is a jumble of worst-case scenarios, each one more terrifying than the last. Rajiv's memories of the torture are disjointed and unclear, but they still have the power to evoke strong emotions. He feels like he's reliving the experience all over again, every time he hears a trigger or sees someone who reminds him of his captors. The name of one of his tormentors is particularly potent, sending shivers down his spine whenever he hears it. As Rajiv navigates this minefield of triggers and memories, he becomes increasingly withdrawn. He stops going to work, unable to face the crowds and chaos that come with being a journalist. His relationships suffer, too, as friends and family grow tired of his erratic behavior and constant cancellations. Rajiv feels like he's losing himself in the process, becoming a shadow of the person he used to be. The cycle is self-reinforcing: Rajiv's negative appraisals fuel his avoidance behaviors, which in turn reinforce his sense of defectiveness and vulnerability. He becomes trapped in this vicious loop, unable to escape the memories that haunt him or shake off the feeling of being constantly on edge. Despite the darkness that surrounds him, Rajiv knows he needs help. The dizziness is getting worse, and he's starting to worry about his own safety. He's reached out to a therapist, hoping to break free from this cycle of fear and self-doubt. As he takes the first tentative steps towards recovery, Rajiv holds onto the hope that one day, he'll be able to confront his demons head-on, without being controlled by them.
